script: The school janitor came to my graduation and sat in the back row where nobody would see him. I did not invite him. My parents did not invite him either, because my parents were not there. My mother left when I was nine and my father worked nights at a plant forty minutes away, which meant that from about the age of eleven I got myself to school and I got myself home. Mr. Alvarez opened the building at five in the morning. I know that because by the time I was twelve I was there at five thirty, waiting by the gym doors, because our apartment had no heat that winter and the school did. He never asked me why I was there so early. He just started unlocking the side door instead of the front one, so I would not have to walk around the whole building in the cold. That was the first thing. The second thing was the food. Our school gave free breakfast until seven fifteen. I was always there before it started, and one morning he handed me a paper bag and said the cafeteria had over ordered. He said that every single morning for four years. A cafeteria does not over order for one thousand four hundred consecutive days. I did not understand that until I was much older. When I was fourteen I got into a fight with a kid who said something about my mother, and I got suspended for three days. Mr. Alvarez found me sitting on the curb outside because I could not go home, because my father would have lost his shift to come get me. He drove me to the public library and told me it opened at nine and closed at eight, and that nobody there asks a kid why he is not in school. He picked me up at eight. All three days. When I was sixteen I told him I was going to drop out and take a full time job at the same plant as my father. He did not argue with me. He did not tell me I was making a mistake. He asked me one question. He asked what my father wanted me to do, and I said my father wanted me to finish, but that we needed the money. Two weeks later a scholarship application appeared in my locker with the deadline circled in pen. I never asked who put it there. I got the scholarship. Four years later I was standing in a gown in a gymnasium that I had spent half my childhood hiding inside, and I looked at the back row, and there he was, in his work shirt, because he had come straight from a shift. He did not clap when they called my name. He just sat there with his hands folded and looked at the floor, the way a man does when he does not think the moment belongs to him. After the ceremony I found him by the door, already picking up programs people had dropped. Still working. Always working. I said his name and he looked up and said congratulations and that he should let me get back to my family. I told him my family was standing right there. He said no, that he was just the guy who opened the doors. So I told him what I had figured out somewhere around my second year of college. I told him that a cafeteria does not over order for four years. I told him I counted, that it was one thousand four hundred and twelve mornings, and that I had known since I was seventeen and had never said anything because I did not know how. He did not say anything at all. He looked at the programs in his hand like he had forgotten they were there. Then he set them down on a chair, which I had never once seen him do, leave something unfinished, and he put his hand over his eyes and stood there in the middle of a gymnasium full of people. My father got there twenty minutes later, still in his work clothes, having driven straight from the plant. I introduced them. My father shook his hand and did not let go of it for a long time. Neither of them said very much. They did not need to. They had been raising the same kid for ten years from opposite ends of the same day.
